item.title: From institutional journalism to political extremes: Structural asymmetries in YouTube's news recommender during the 2022 French presidential campaign
item.description: arXiv:2611.18034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Debate has intensified over how algorithmic recommendations shape news visibility, particularly regarding structural and ideological bias. This study examines YouTube's News Recommender System (NRS) in the French ``News'' section, using a large-scale audit based on automated browsing agents operating under cold-start conditions, without prior viewing history, to isolate the algorithm's structural baseline independently of user preferences. Our results reveal that YouTube's NRS operates within a structurally asymmetric visibility regime: even in the absence of prior user behaviour, recommendation outputs disproportionately privilege platform-native creators and politically engaged content over established journalism. Television channels retain some relative advantage, but institutional news outlets, particularly press and radio, are systematically marginalised across recommendation sequences. Among political content, figures affiliated with far-left and far-right movements occupy a disproportionately visible position in recommendation outputs. Rather than correcting this asymmetry, continuity effects reproduce and stabilise it across recommendation sequences. These results show that visibility in YouTube's News section cannot be reduced to accumulated user preferences alone, but is also shaped by a structural bias embedded in the platform's recommendation system, which plays an important role in sustaining the prominence of political actors affiliated with the far left and far right.
item.dc:creator: Julien Figeac (UTOPI), Erwan Le Merrer (ARTISHAU), Marie Neihouser (CESSP), Gilles Tr{\'e}dan (LAAS-TRUST)

item.title: Majority Illusions in Large Random Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.22132v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent in a social network is under majority illusion when the majority among its neighbors differs from the majority in the whole network. We study analytically the probability of the occurrence of majority illusions on large random networks. We derive 0-1 laws for graph sequences that locally converge, using different types of random opinion-assignment functions. Our results show that in large random networks with uniform random opinion-assignment the probability of majority illusions goes to 0. However, when opinions depend on nodes' degrees the probability may go to 1. From a methodological point of view, our work illustrates how local convergence techniques from probability theory can be effectively applied to the understanding of opinion-related phenomena---such as majority illusions---in large networks.
item.dc:creator: Maaike Venema-Los, Zo\'e Christoff, Serte Donderwinkel, Davide Grossi

item.title: Efficiently Estimating Cycle Statistics on Graphs via Spanning Trees
item.description: arXiv:2611.07925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simple cycles encode feedback and alternative routes in networks and are important for routing problems, the convergence of dynamical processes on networks, message passing and belief propagation, or even static network characterizations such as structural balance in signed networks. Being able to assess and sample from the cycle structure of a graph is thus of interest in many analysis contexts. However, due to the combinatorial growth of the cycle space with graph size, the computational cost for such sampling is high. Therefore, we here introduce a sampling framework that enables us to sample from the cycle structure without enumerating all cycles. Specifically, the method draws uniform spanning trees and collects the fundamental cycles created by their non-tree edges, such that each tree provides an informative subset of simple cycles. Because cycles are included with unequal probabilities and are dependent within each subset, we formulate an inclusion-probability-based Horvitz-Thompson estimator, which we average over random subsets, a procedure we call Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson. For this, we sample multiple Horvitz-Thompson estimators and introduce a method to further subsample the individual estimators for increased computational performance. For sampling cycles, the estimator is unbiased if exact cycle inclusion probabilities are known. To extend the method to larger networks, we derive an efficient mean-field approximation for the inclusion probabilities and characterize the graph regimes in which it remains accurate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate the computational scaling and statistical performance of the framework. We then illustrate the utility of Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson estimation by estimating cycle counts and cycle-level frustration statistics in signed spin systems. An implementation is available in the py-raccoon package.
item.dc:creator: Josef Hoppe, Michael T. Schaub

item.title: HyBridge: Bridge-Guided Self-Supervised Hyperbolic Hypergraph Representation Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.16351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypergraphs capture groupwise relationships among multiple nodes and often exhibit tree-like structures. Although hyperbolic space is well suited for modeling such structures, simply extending existing hypergraph representation learning (HRL) methods to hyperbolic space does not consistently improve performance. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between node structural properties and hyperbolic embedding radii and find that bridge nodes tend to lie closer to the center in graphs, whereas this relationship is not consistently observed in hypergraphs. We further find that conventional bridge score estimation may fail to capture the groupwise connectivity of hypergraphs. Motivated by these findings, we propose HyBridge, a self-supervised hyperbolic HRL framework that (1) estimates node bridge scores by considering the external connectivity of individual hyperedges, (2) learns node and hyperedge embeddings through hyperbolic hypergraph encoding, (3) guides node radial positions according to their bridge scores, and (4) employs contrastive learning to preserve node discriminability. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world hypergraphs demonstrate that HyBridge outperforms 22 competing methods, achieving performance improvements of up to 9.82% in node classification. For reproducibility, we provide the code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HyBridge/.
item.dc:creator: So-Bin Jung, David Yoon Suk, Sang-Wook Kim

item.title: Random Abstract Cell Complexes
item.description: arXiv:2406.01999v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In machine learning and signal processing, methods based on (abstract) cell complexes (CCs) are being applied successfully in different applications. However, there is currently a lack of random models, which are necessary for a thorough evaluation of these methods, both by generating synthetic data and as null models to compare results to. We fill this gap by defining a random model for abstract cell complexes based on independent inclusion probabilities, similar to the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model for graphs. We also discuss how modifications to bias the model to incorporate more structure can be implemented. The model can also be used to lift a graph (or other cell complex) to a cell complex of arbitrary dimension. The main challenge in this is that the number of cycles (possible 2-cells) on graphs is exponential, and the same is true in higher dimensions. We overcome this complexity with an approximate sampling algorithm limited to 2-cells (polygons) that is based on a recent advance in sampling cycles on a graph. Using this algorithm, we analyze the properties of random 2-dimensional CCs and showcase its usage as a performance baseline for both topological signal processing and topological deep learning. The algorithm is available in the package py-raccoon on the Python Package Index.
item.dc:creator: Josef Hoppe, Michael T. Schaub

item.title: Curating Safe Spaces for Emotion Disclosure during Illness Recovery on Video-Sharing Platforms
item.description: arXiv:2502.20658v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The advent of video-sharing platforms has transformed self-expression, transcending entertainment to encompass sensitive disclosures and emotional revelations. In this submission, we discuss our study on emotional disclosure by individuals with Schizophrenia through YouTube vlogs and its implications for designing safe online spaces.
item.dc:creator: Jiaying "Lizzy" Liu, Yunlong Wang, Allen Jue, Yao Lyu, Yiheng Su, Shuo Niu, Nathan TeBlunthuis, Yan Zhang

item.title: Chi-Square Wavelet Graph Neural Networks for Heterogeneous Graph Anomaly Detection
item.description: arXiv:2505.18934v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD) in heterogeneous networks presents unique challenges due to node and edge heterogeneity. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN) methods primarily focus on homogeneous GAD and thus fail to address three key issues: (C1) Capturing abnormal signal and rich semantics across diverse meta-paths; (C2) Retaining high-frequency content in HIN dimension alignment; and (C3) Learning effectively from difficult anomaly samples with class imbalance. To overcome these, we propose ChiGAD, a spectral GNN framework based on a novel Chi-Square filter, inspired by the wavelet effectiveness in diverse domains. Specifically, ChiGAD consists of: (1) Multi-Graph Chi-Square Filter, which captures anomalous information via applying dedicated Chi-Square filters to each meta-path graph; (2) Interactive Meta-Graph Convolution, which aligns features while preserving high-frequency information and incorporates heterogeneous messages by a unified Chi-Square Filter; and (3) Contribution-Informed Cross-Entropy Loss, which prioritizes difficult anomalies to address class imbalance. Extensive experiments on public and industrial datasets show that ChiGAD outperforms state-of-the-art models on multiple metrics. Additionally, its homogeneous variant, ChiGNN, excels on seven GAD datasets, validating the effectiveness of Chi-Square filters. Our code is available at https://github.com/HsipingLi/ChiGAD.
item.dc:creator: Xiping Li, Xiangyu Dong, Xingyi Zhang, Kun Xie, Yuanhao Feng, Bo Wang, Guilin Li, Wuxiong Zeng, Xiujun Shu, Sibo Wang
